question.prompt: Ten women sit in \(10\) seats in a line. All of the \(10\) get up and then reseat themselves using all \(10\) seats, each sitting in the seat she was in before or a seat next to the one she occupied before. In how many ways can the women be reseated?

solutions.explanation:
Number the women by their original seats, from left to right. Let \(a_n\) be the number of legal reseatings for \(n\) women in \(n\) consecutive seats under the same rule.

The first woman has only two possibilities. If she stays in seat \(1\), the remaining women have \(a_{n-1}\) legal arrangements in the remaining seats. If she moves to seat \(2\), then the second woman must occupy seat \(1\): no other woman can reach that seat. These two women swap, leaving \(a_{n-2}\) arrangements for the remaining women.

The cases are disjoint and cover every legal reseating. Moreover, every legal arrangement of the remaining women extends in exactly one way within its case. Therefore, for \(n\ge2\),
\[
a_n=a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}.
\]
There is one arrangement of no women and one arrangement of a single woman, so \(a_0=a_1=1\). Successively adding the preceding two counts gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_2&=2,&a_3&=3,&a_4&=5,\\
a_5&=8,&a_6&=13,&a_7&=21,\\
a_8&=34,&a_9&=55,&a_{10}&=89.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus there are \(\boxed{89}\) reseatings, choice \(\boxed{\text{A}}\).
solutions.title: Count by the first woman’s choice

solutions.explanation:
Every legal reseating consists of women who stay and disjoint adjacent pairs who swap. To prove this, start at the leftmost woman not yet considered. She either stays, or moves one seat right. In the latter case, her neighbor must move into her old seat, since no later woman can reach it. Remove that single woman or swapped pair and repeat along the line.

Suppose there are \(k\) swapped pairs, where \(0\le k\le5\). Treat each swapped pair as a double block and each woman who stays as a single block. There are \(k\) double blocks and \(10-2k\) single blocks, making \(10-k\) blocks altogether. Choosing which \(k\) of those block positions are double determines the reseating, giving
\[
\binom{10-k}{k}
\]
possibilities.

This correspondence is reversible: read the blocks from left to right, assign the next original woman to a single block, and swap the next two original women in a double block. Thus every reseating is counted once. Different values of \(k\) are disjoint cases, so the total is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{k=0}^{5}\binom{10-k}{k}
&=1+9+28+35+15+1\\
&=\boxed{89}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The answer is \(\boxed{\text{A}}\).
solutions.title: Count blocks of adjacent swaps
